summary: Specifies how DCCP can use the Quick-Start mechanism, in which a sender may be allowed to begin with a higher initial rate. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: Normally a new driver crawls at first to see how busy the road is. Quick-Start lets routers say the road is empty, so you can go faster.

subtitle: Allowing faster initial sending rates when the network permits.

tldr.problem: Most data flows start slowly to probe the network's available capacity, a process that may be unnecessary if the network path has spare bandwidth. A faster start-up would benefit applications like streaming media and online games.
tldr.mechanism: Quick-Start allows a DCCP sender to request a higher initial sending rate from routers along the path. If all routers approve, the receiver confirms, and the sender transmits at the approved rate for a limited time while monitoring for congestion.
tldr.outcome: Flows can begin transmission faster if the network has available capacity, improving user experience. However, false positives and deployment barriers limit Quick-Start to controlled environments.

today: RFC 5634 remains Experimental and is not recommended for general Internet use. Quick-Start's utility is limited by poor router support and middlebox interference. It is practical only in managed networks where the administrator controls routers and can verify Quick-Start support.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) is a transport protocol for applications that need congestion control but tolerate occasional packet loss, such as streaming media, voice over IP, and online games. Unlike TCP, which guarantees reliable, ordered delivery, DCCP is datagram-based and allows the application to choose among different congestion control identifiers (CCIDs).

This RFC specifies how DCCP can use the Quick-Start mechanism defined in RFC 4782. Quick-Start allows a DCCP sender to cooperate with routers along the network path to determine a higher initial sending rate at the start of a connection, and also during the connection (e.g., after an idle period). This avoids the usual slow-start phase, which probes for available bandwidth by starting at a very low rate.

The specification is experimental and intended for use in controlled environments (such as a campus network or a single organization's infrastructure), not for general Internet deployment.
sections.eli5: DCCP is like UDP but with traffic control built in: it lets you send stuff quickly but backs off if the network gets congested. Quick-Start asks the network "is it OK to go fast?" and starts faster if the answer is yes.

sections.title: Quick-Start Operation
sections.content:
A DCCP sender begins a Quick-Start request by including a Quick-Start option in an IP header (or IPv6 extension header) of a DCCP packet. The option includes a desired sending rate in bytes per second.

Each router supporting Quick-Start along the path can approve the rate, reduce it, or reject it entirely. If any router rejects it, the sender receives no approval. If all routers approve (possibly with rate reductions), the DCCP receiver examines the request and responds with a Quick-Start Response, a new DCCP header option that carries the approved rate.

Upon receiving approval, the sender enters Quick-Start Mode, where it sends packets at the approved rate for up to one round-trip time (RTT). After this period, it enters the Quick-Start Validation Phase, a unique feature for DCCP that lasts up to two RTTs. During validation, the sender confirms that the network can sustain the rate without congestion.

If congestion is detected during either phase, the sender immediately reverts to its standard congestion control mechanism and the Quick-Start attempt fails.
sections.eli5: Sender asks routers: "Can I send at 1 Mbps?" Routers say yes or reduce it. Receiver approves. Sender goes fast for a while, watching for trouble. If things break, it slows down.

sections.title: Integration with Congestion Control Identifiers
sections.content:
DCCP supports multiple congestion control algorithms, each identified by a CCID. RFC 5634 specifies how Quick-Start integrates with three CCIDs:

CCID 2 uses a TCP-like window-based mechanism. When Quick-Start approves a rate, the sender calculates a QS_cwnd (Quick-Start congestion window) and paces packets at the approved rate. The sender must implement rate pacing because TCP-like algorithms do not inherently pace transmissions.

CCID 3 and CCID 4 use rate-based congestion control inspired by TFRC (TCP-Friendly Rate Control). For these, the sender sets a QS_sendrate based on the approved rate. These protocols are already rate-paced, so the sender directly uses the rate.

For all CCIDs, if no loss or congestion is reported during the validation phase, the sender exits Quick-Start and continues with standard congestion control. If loss or congestion is detected at any point, the sender reduces its rate according to the CCID's rules and abandons the Quick-Start attempt.
sections.eli5: Different CCIDs handle the approved rate differently: one works like TCP (watches a window), two work like a rate meter (watches bytes per second). All monitor for problems and bail out if they find them.

sections.title: Rate Requests and Validation
sections.content:
A sender should request a Quick-Start rate that reflects what it actually intends to send, not an inflated request hoping for a discount. Overestimating depletes the bandwidth pool maintained by Quick-Start routers, potentially blocking legitimate later requests.

DCCP applications often have a natural media rate they wish to achieve (e.g., a video stream at a specific bitrate). The sender should request approximately this rate (adjusted for header overhead), which aligns the Quick-Start request with actual transmission intentions.

The Quick-Start Interval prevents excessive use of Quick-Start. After the first request, the interval starts at 6 seconds (minimum). After each unsuccessful request, the interval doubles (exponential backoff), capping at 64 seconds. After the interval exceeds 64 seconds, the sender stops using Quick-Start for the remainder of the connection. When a request is approved, the interval resets to 6 seconds.

Path changes (detected through mobility signals) may reset the interval, allowing the sender to probe again after the network topology has shifted.
sections.eli5: Only ask for the speed you actually need. Don't spam requests: wait longer between attempts if they fail. If the network changes, try again.

sections.title: Limitations and Experimental Status
sections.content:
Quick-Start has significant limitations that restrict it to controlled environments. Many routers in the public Internet do not support Quick-Start, so requests fail silently. IP options and extension headers are sometimes dropped or blocked by middleboxes, preventing the request from reaching the receiver.

Quick-Start can produce false positives: the sender might believe the request was approved when routers have silently dropped the option. Paths using IP tunnels, MPLS, or multi-access Layer 2 networks often cannot support Quick-Start effectively.

For CCID 2, approval of a higher rate can increase control traffic on the reverse path, potentially congesting the return link and limiting forward throughput. CCID 3 and CCID 4 send feedback only once per RTT, so return-path impact is minimal.

Due to these challenges, RFC 5634 specifies that Quick-Start is suitable only for controlled, single-organization networks where administrators can ensure routers and middleboxes support it correctly. Widespread deployment on the general Internet is not recommended.
sections.eli5: The internet is messy: some routers don't know about Quick-Start, some drop the request, some say yes when they shouldn't. So you can only use it in networks you control.
